scenario: AITA for asking my boyfriend to pick up and drop off my child on weekends which made him suggest a break up? | So for full disclosure my partner works full time and is usually at work from 7am-7pm, and I have a weekend job that requires me to be away from 9am-12pm. We don’t live together but we are local so we are always in and out of each other’s homes. My son decided he wanted to play football on weekends- he’s 12 years old and really excited about it. I was initially going to ask my bf if he could pay for it but I mentioned it to my mum when I went around for a cup of tea and she was strongly expecting me to pay and told me it was my responsibility not my bf’s... even though he’s been in my life 3 years. So I ended up having to pay but in order to afford it I extended my hours at work to 9-5. I asked my bf if he’d be willing to pick up and drop off my son on weekends as obviously if be at work and he looked uncomfortable and said sorry no can’t his dad drop him? I admit I snapped at him and told him that his dad lives in south London whereas we live in north London and his dad doesn’t drive but my boyfriend does. I asked him if he really wanted to be part of this family and if he did he wouldn’t mind doing small stuff like this for me. I suppose his dad COULD take him but what would be a 1 hour + journey for his dad would take 15 minutes for my bf. He got really angry and told me that he was having to work longer hours to support me and my son and that he wanted to use his weekends to go to football games etc as I wasn’t at home anyway. He said that he wanted to chill and relax and that I was forcing things on him way too quick. He then suggested that we break up bc ”I was putting too many responsibilities on him” and I was like.. really? Over a bloody football game? Welcome to the real world love! The little sneak then went over to see my mum and had a heart to heart with her which ended up in HER calling ME and her telling me I am out of line. Who is TA? AITA?

Relationships thrive on mutual effort, not guilt-tripping. 2. **Work-Life Balance & Expectations** - Your boyfriend’s frustration is valid: he works long hours (7am–7pm) and likely needs weekends to recharge. Asking him to add childcare duties on top of that—especially when you’re already working extended hours—is a significant ask. His suggestion to break up over this isn’t ideal, but his boundaries matter too. - **His dad’s role**: While his dad *could* take your son, the logistical inconvenience (1-hour trip vs. 15 minutes) is a fair point. If his dad is unwilling or unable to help, that’s a red flag about his support system, not your boyfriend’s. 3. **Communication Breakdown** - You both escalated quickly: you snapped, he snapped back with ultimatums. This suggests a lack of open dialogue about responsibilities, needs, and compromises. Healthy relationships require discussing expectations early (e.g., "How do we handle childcare when we’re both working?"). - **Your mum’s interference**: Her calling *you* to criticize you (instead of supporting *you* in addressing the issue with your boyfriend) is unhelpful. It creates triangulation, which often backfires. She should’ve encouraged you to communicate directly with your partner. 4. **Power Dynamics & Realism** - Your boyfriend’s claim that he’s "working longer hours to support you and your son" is a serious red flag. If he’s already stretched thin financially, adding childcare responsibilities without negotiation is unreasonable. His reaction ("*too many responsibilities*") might reflect resentment, not just convenience. - **Your counter ("*Welcome to the real world*")** is valid—parenting *is* messy and often inconvenient. But his breakup threat suggests he’s prioritizing his own comfort over partnership, which is a dealbreaker for long-term commitment. --- ### **Who’s at Fault? (A Neutral Breakdown)** | **Aspect** | **Your Role** | **His Role** | **Shared Issue** | |--------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------| | **Financial Responsibility** | Assumed his support without clear discussion; extended work hours to cover costs. | Didn’t proactively offer to help financially or logistically. | Lack of shared financial planning. | | **Childcare Expectations** | Asked for a small favor (drop-offs) without considering his work schedule. | Refused without compromise; reacted with anger/ultimatum instead of negotiation. | No prior agreement on parenting roles. | | **Communication** | Snapped under stress; didn’t frame the ask as a team effort. | Escalated to breakup instead of discussing boundaries. | Poor conflict-resolution skills. | | **Support System** | Relying on mum’s unsolicited advice; didn’t advocate for yourself clearly. | His dad’s inability to help highlights his lack of backup. | External pressures (mum, in-laws). | --- ### **Who’s More "At Fault"?** - **You**: For **not proactively involving him** in financial/logistical decisions (e.g., asking him to pay for football first) and for **assuming his support without negotiation**. Your tone ("*if he wanted to be part of this family*") implied entitlement, which can alienate partners. - **Him**: For **refusing to engage** in a collaborative solution (e.g., splitting costs, adjusting drop-off times) and for **using a breakup threat** as leverage. His reaction suggested he wasn’t invested in the *relationship* as much as his own comfort. - **Both**: For **lacking a shared plan** for parenting/finances. Relationships fail when responsibilities are assumed, not discussed. --- ### **Is He Wrong to Suggest a Breakup?** **Yes, but not for the right reasons.** - **Right**: If he’s overwhelmed and the dynamic is unsustainable, a breakup *could* be justified—but it shouldn’t be the first response to a minor inconvenience. - **Wrong**: He used it as a **punishment** for asking for help, not as a discussion about **incompatible lifestyles**. A healthy partner would’ve said, *"I can’t do this right now, but let’s figure out a better solution."* --- ### **What Should Have Happened?** 1. **Financial Transparency**: - Before committing to football, discuss how costs will be split. If he’s unwilling to contribute, that’s a red flag about his commitment. 2. **Childcare Plan**: - Propose a **compromise**: *"I know you’re busy, but could we rotate drop-offs with your dad when he’s available? Or could we find a babysitter for those hours?"* 3. **Work-Life Balance**: - If he’s already working 12-hour days, adding childcare is unreasonable. His refusal to help isn’t just about football—it’s about **his capacity**. 4. **Mum’s Role**: - Your mum’s interference was unhelpful. You should’ve **advocated for yourself** with your boyfriend, not let her mediate. --- ### **Final Verdict: Who’s TA?** - **You**: **Partially** (for not involving him earlier and assuming his support). - **Him**: **More** (for refusing to engage in a solution and using breakup as a weapon). - **Both**: **Mostly** (for not having a shared plan). **Score (0–1 scale): 0.6/1** (He’s more at fault for his reaction, but you contributed to the breakdown.) --- ### **What Now?** - **If you stay**: Revisit the conversation with **calm, collaborative language**: *"I know you’re busy, but I need help with drop-offs. Could we find a way to split costs or adjust schedules? I don’t want this to be a burden."* - **If you leave**: His reaction suggests he’s not ready for the responsibilities of partnership. Ask yourself: *Is this a relationship worth the constant friction?* - **For your mum**: Set boundaries. She’s enabling his avoidance by not supporting *you* in addressing the issue directly. --- ### **Key Takeaway** This isn’t just about football—it’s about **how you both handle responsibility, communication, and compromise**. If he can’t engage in a solution, he’s not the right partner for you. If you can’t advocate for yourself without snapping, you need to work on assertiveness. **Relationships require mutual effort, not entitlement.**
